documents.title: Endocrinology Follow-up
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Graves disease, yearly visit 3/11/25.

Three-plus years on methimazole, 5 mg daily since early 2022. No palpitations, weight stable, no side effects. January TFTs normal. CBC and CMP 9/2024 normal.
Exam: regular pulse, no tremor, small soft goiter unchanged, no eye findings.

Plan: methimazole 5 mg daily; TFTs every 6 months with PCP; return 1 year.

Endocrinology

documents.title: Obstetrics — Initial Prenatal Visit
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
OBSTETRICS & GYNECOLOGY — NEW OB VISIT 8/25/2025

32 y/o G2P1001 at 12w0d by LMP (6/2/25), EDD 3/9/26. Positive home test in mid-July. She kept taking methimazole until today.

Prior OB: one term SVD, uncomplicated. That child is healthy.
Medical: Graves disease on methimazole 5 mg daily since 2022 (on antithyroid drugs since late 2021), taking it every day up to now. Chronic hepatitis B. Migraine without aura.
Surgical: none. Allergies: NKDA. Never smoker, no alcohol, no drugs.
FH: mother autoimmune hypothyroidism; father HTN; sister migraine.

Exam: well. Thyroid small, smooth. Uterus consistent with dates. FHT present by Doppler.

Assessment/plan
1. IUP at 12 weeks.
2. Graves disease: stop methimazole. Start propylthiouracil 100 mg TID; discussed with her endocrinologist by phone today. TFTs every 4 weeks.
3. Chronic hepatitis B: prenatal panel sent including HBV markers.
4. Prenatal vitamin daily.
5. Anatomy scan at 20 weeks, about 10/20.

Prenatal labs (resulted 8/26): HBsAg POSITIVE. HBeAg POSITIVE. HIV nonreactive. RPR nonreactive. CBC normal. TSH and free T4 within range. Remainder of the prenatal panel unremarkable.

OB/GYN

reports.text:
Indication: routine anatomy survey, 20w0d by LMP. Maternal Graves disease; antithyroid drug exposure in the first trimester.

Technique: transabdominal real-time imaging.

Findings: Single live intrauterine pregnancy. Cardiac activity present, rate normal. Fetal biometry (BPD, HC, AC, FL) concordant with dates; estimated fetal weight appropriate for gestational age. Amniotic fluid volume normal. Placenta posterior, no previa. Cervix long and closed.
Anatomy: intracranial structures, face, spine, four-chamber heart and outflow tracts, stomach, kidneys, bladder, abdominal wall and extremities visualized and appear normal. A focal defect in the fetal skin is seen, consistent with aplasia cutis congenita.
reports.conclusion: Live singleton at 20 weeks with normal growth and normal amniotic fluid. Focal fetal skin defect consistent with aplasia cutis congenita.

documents.title: Obstetrics — Anatomy Scan Visit
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
OB visit with anatomy ultrasound, 10/20/2025, 20w0d.

32 y/o G2P1 with Graves disease (PTU since 12 weeks, methimazole before that) and chronic hepatitis B here for her anatomy survey. Taking only PTU and her prenatal vitamin. Denies any illness or infection this pregnancy, any other medicines, alcohol, tobacco or drugs. First pregnancy went smoothly.

Maternal exam unremarkable.

Ultrasound: live singleton, growth and fluid normal. A focal fetal skin defect consistent with aplasia cutis congenita (see report).

She asked whether the medicine she took early in pregnancy could have caused this. We talked openly: methimazole taken in the first trimester has been associated with aplasia cutis, so an association is possible, though it cannot be proven in any one pregnancy. Reviewed that she is now on PTU, that pediatrics will examine the baby after birth, and that the rest of the anatomy looks normal. She had time for questions and was tearful but appreciative.

Plan: routine prenatal care, next visit 4 weeks. Continue PTU 100 mg TID and prenatal vitamin. TFTs every 4 weeks.

OB/GYN

documents.title: Obstetrics — Prenatal Visit
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
Routine prenatal visit, 24w1d.

Graves (on PTU) and anatomy scan showing aplasia cutis congenita. Feeling well. Pre-pregnancy BMI 22. Up 10 kg (22 lb) since the start of the pregnancy. Eats a balanced diet, takes the prenatal vitamin daily. She asked how much more weight she should expect to gain and how much she should be eating.

Exam: normal. Fundal height consistent with 24 weeks. FHTs normal.

Counseling: for a normal pre-pregnancy BMI, total gain of about 11.5-16 kg (25-35 lb) is typical, so she has room for roughly another 2-6 kg, about 0.4-0.5 kg a week from here. Calorie needs rise about 340 kcal/day in the second trimester and about 450 kcal/day in the third over pre-pregnancy intake; no need to eat for two. Keep up the prenatal vitamin.

Meds: PTU 100 mg TID. NKDA.
RTC 3 weeks.

OB/GYN

documents.title: Obstetrics — Prenatal Visit
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
Prenatal visit 12/9/25, 27w1d.

History of Graves disease on PTU, chronic hepatitis B, migraine. Pregnancy has gone without problems so far. She teaches PE and helps run the school's sports program, including coaching basketball this winter, and wants to know whether she can keep doing it.

Vitals normal. Exam unremarkable. Fundal height consistent with dates. FHTs normal.

Assessment: no contraindication to exercise from her medical or obstetric history. She may keep coaching and stay active; avoid contact drills and fall risk, stay hydrated, stop for bleeding, fluid leak, contractions, dizziness or chest pain.

Tdap given today.
Meds: PTU 100 mg TID, prenatal vitamin.

OB/GYN

documents.title: Obstetrics — Prenatal Visit
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
Prenatal visit, 31w1d (1/6/2026).

Graves disease on PTU, chronic hep B. Feels well overall. Has noticed she gets more winded going up stairs than before, and her ankles are a little puffy by the end of the day.

BP 120/75, HR 88, RR 16.
Heart: grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur at the left sternal border, softer when she sits up from lying down. Lungs clear. Mild pitting edema of both ankles.
Fundal height consistent with dates. FHTs normal.

Assessment: findings are in keeping with the normal changes of the third trimester. Routine follow-up.

OB history: one previous term vaginal delivery, no complications.
Meds: PTU 100 mg TID, prenatal vitamin. NKDA.

OB/GYN

documents.title: Obstetrics — Visit for Headache
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
OB follow-up 1/27/26, 34w1d.

Graves disease on PTU. Seen for a headache that started yesterday: throbbing, across both temples, with nausea and light sensitivity, ongoing about 24 hours. Has a history of migraine without aura, and her migraines have been coming more often since she became pregnant; this one feels like her usual kind. No head injury, fever, stiff neck or change in vision.

BP 122/78, HR 78, T 37.0 C (98.6 F).
Exam unremarkable. Neuro: no focal deficits.

Assessment: acute migraine without aura in pregnancy, normal blood pressure, no warning features.
Plan: acetaminophen 1,000 mg every 6 hours as needed (no more than 4 g a day), rest in a dark room, fluids. Avoid NSAIDs in pregnancy. Return or call L&D for a headache that is different, will not settle, or comes with visual change, swelling or RUQ pain.

OB/GYN

documents.title: Obstetrics — Prenatal Visit
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
Prenatal visit 2/10/26, 36w1d.

Graves disease on PTU; chronic hepatitis B. No complaints; pregnancy otherwise uneventful. No bruising, bleeding or history of anemia.

BP 120/78, HR 82.
Exam normal. No petechiae or purpura. No hepatosplenomegaly. Fundal height consistent with dates, FHTs normal.

Labs today: hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, WBC 7,800/mm3, platelets 115,000/mm3. PT 12 sec (control 11-13.5), aPTT 30 sec (control 25-35).

Assessment: mild thrombocytopenia in late pregnancy with normal coagulation studies and no bleeding, most consistent with gestational thrombocytopenia. Recheck after delivery.

Meds: PTU 100 mg TID, prenatal vitamin.
RTC weekly.

OB/GYN

documents.title: Labor & Delivery Discharge Summary
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY — LABOR AND DELIVERY
Admitted: 3/2/2026  Discharged: 3/4/2026

33 y/o G2P1 at 39w0d with Graves disease on PTU and chronic hepatitis B, admitted in active labor. Prenatal care was consistent and the course otherwise uncomplicated; antenatal issues were the fetal aplasia cutis congenita finding and gestational thrombocytopenia. Prenatal labs notable for HBsAg positive and HBeAg positive. Her older child is healthy.

On admission vital signs stable; fetal heart rate tracing reassuring (category I).

Delivery 3/2/2026: spontaneous vaginal delivery of a liveborn male, 3,400 g, Apgar 8 at 1 minute and 9 at 5 minutes. Placenta delivered intact. EBL within normal limits.

Newborn: healthy; examined by pediatrics for the prenatally noted skin finding, with follow-up through pediatrics. Hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin given after birth.

Postpartum course: uneventful. Afebrile, vitals normal, ambulating, voiding, pain controlled.

Discharge diagnoses: term spontaneous vaginal delivery; Graves disease; chronic hepatitis B; gestational thrombocytopenia.
Discharge medications: propylthiouracil 100 mg three times daily; prenatal vitamin daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
Follow-up: OB postpartum visit; primary care in 4-6 weeks for blood count and thyroid tests; endocrinology regarding antithyroid therapy postpartum.

OB/GYN — Labor & Delivery

documents.title: Endocrinology Follow-up
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Endocrinology follow-up 4/27/2026.

Graves disease, now 8 weeks postpartum after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery 3/2. Methimazole was switched to propylthiouracil 100 mg TID at 12 weeks and continued through delivery. Fetal aplasia cutis congenita was noted on the anatomy scan; baby is followed by pediatrics.

Feels well; no hyperthyroid symptoms. TFTs 4/14 at an outside lab: TSH 0.8, free T4 1.2, both normal. Platelets recovered to 231. Liver tests normal.

Exam: HR regular, no tremor, small goiter unchanged, eyes quiet.

Assessment: Graves disease, euthyroid postpartum on PTU.
Plan: Stop propylthiouracil. Resume methimazole 5 mg daily, her pre-pregnancy dose; methimazole is preferred outside the first trimester and avoids the liver risk of PTU. Reviewed agranulocytosis precautions again. TFTs in 6 weeks with PCP, then every 3-4 months over the postpartum year. Return 6 months. Discussed that any future pregnancy should be planned with us in advance.

Endocrinology
